question: Can increasingly aggressive selection of informative examples from increasingly large source datasets create a retained-data Pareto frontier that improves faster than conventional power-law error scaling?

key_findings.claim: In a teacher-student perceptron, retaining low-margin examples can turn a retained-sample Pareto envelope from power-law into at least exponential error decay.
key_findings.evidence: For every fixed retained fraction, asymptotic error remains proportional to inverse retained sample size; the faster envelope arises by jointly increasing the source pool and decreasing the fraction retained so each selected example stays near the teacher boundary.

key_findings.claim: Imperfect selection creates a crossover back to power-law behavior.
key_findings.evidence: When the probe boundary differs from the teacher by nonzero angle, theory predicts a minimum useful retention fraction; a weak four-epoch probe on SVHN exhibits this lower envelope while a stronger 40-epoch probe delays it.

key_findings.claim: Vision experiments reproduce qualitative signatures of the theory, but the strongest practical ImageNet result is modest pruning rather than demonstrated exponential scaling at foundation scale.
key_findings.evidence: ResNet sweeps on SVHN, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet show better fitted Pareto curves as source size and pruning vary; the scalable prototype metric removes 20% of ImageNet with near-baseline top-5 accuracy, not orders-of-magnitude data reduction.

key_findings.claim: The self-supervised prototype score is a cheap and competitive ImageNet pruning heuristic under the paper's accounting.
key_findings.evidence: Cosine distance to the nearest k-means centroid in a pretrained SWaV embedding matches or exceeds memorization until roughly 70-80% remains and is robust to an order-of-magnitude variation in cluster count.

anchors.section: F Impact of number of clusters

key_findings.claim: 'Beating data scaling' depends on counting retained training examples rather than all examples acquired, scored, or used to train the probe.
key_findings.evidence: A point on the Pareto frontier with alpha_prune examples is selected from alpha_total greater than alpha_prune and may require a learned scoring model; the x-axis omits this upstream data access and selection computation, so it is not an end-to-end sample- or compute-scaling law.

key_findings.claim: Selection changes the training distribution and can amplify imbalance and fairness risks.
key_findings.evidence: Every ImageNet metric increases class imbalance, necessitating a 50% balancing rule; appendix audits show a small systematic reduction for harder classes and the authors caution that deployment-specific fairness tests remain necessary.

method.core_idea: Rank a large source pool by estimated informativeness, train on a retained subset, and choose both source-pool size and retained fraction to minimize error at each retained-data budget.
method.mechanism: Solve margin pruning in a replica teacher-student perceptron, connect selected examples to posterior information gain, sweep source size and retention fraction in vision models, benchmark supervised scores, and introduce centroid distance in self-supervised embeddings as a scalable score.
assumptions: A probe score is closely aligned with the unknown target decision boundary.
Retained-example count is the relevant data resource even when the source pool and probe are larger.
Perceptron margin theory predicts qualitative deep-network behavior.
Class balancing can repair selection-induced distribution distortion without eliminating gains.
A pretrained representation used for scoring is available and its cost can be amortized.

techniques.role: Optimizes source size and retained fraction for every final training-set budget.
Provides a solvable model of selecting examples near a decision boundary.
Explains faster retained-data scaling through nonvanishing information per selected example.
Scores images by distance to centroids in SWaV embedding space.
Mitigates label-frequency distortion introduced by difficulty pruning.

evaluations.setting: Analytic and simulated high-dimensional teacher-student perceptron.
evaluations.metric: Generalization error and information gain versus retained examples.
evaluations.result: Perfect margin ranking yields an at-least-exponential Pareto envelope; probe error creates a later power-law crossover.
evaluations.baseline: Random selection and every fixed retained fraction.

evaluations.setting: ResNet-18 on SVHN and CIFAR-10 across source sizes and pruning fractions.
evaluations.metric: Test error scaling with retained examples.
evaluations.result: EL2N-selected Pareto envelopes qualitatively beat unpruned power-law fits over the tested ranges.

evaluations.metric: Top-5 validation accuracy and scaling curves.
evaluations.result: Memorization and prototype scores retain near-full accuracy at about 80% of the data; many small-dataset scores scale poorly.
evaluations.baseline: Eight supervised pruning metrics, random pruning, and full-data training.

evaluations.setting: Transfer learning between ImageNet and CIFAR-10.
evaluations.metric: Downstream accuracy after pruning fine-tuning or pretraining data.
evaluations.result: Ten percent of CIFAR-10 can suffice for a pretrained ViT, and pretraining on 50% of selected ImageNet can match downstream full-ImageNet pretraining.
evaluations.baseline: Fine-tuning or pretraining on all available examples.

evaluations.setting: ImageNet robustness, class accuracy, longer training, and cluster-count appendices.
evaluations.metric: OOD accuracy, human-consistency measures, per-class accuracy, top-5 accuracy, and training time.
evaluations.result: Moderate pruning is broadly stable, but class balancing and resource-accounting choices materially affect conclusions.
evaluations.baseline: Unpruned training and multiple pruning fractions/settings.

limitations: Author-stated: exponential scaling requires an unusually high-quality pruning score; many existing metrics fail to scale to ImageNet.
Author-stated: matching full-data iterations can reduce the training-time advantage, though gains saturate before equal time in their study.
Author-stated: class balancing is essential and its amount lacks a principled selection rule.
Reviewer inference: retained-data scaling excludes source acquisition, storage, scoring, and probe-training costs.
Reviewer inference: selecting each Pareto point after seeing many curves risks optimistic envelope estimation unless selection is nested and prospective.
Reviewer inference: the deep-network evidence spans a limited log range and does not establish an asymptotic exponential law for modern foundation-model pretraining.
failure_modes: A score overselects outliers, mislabeled points, or minority classes and shifts the objective away from deployment risk.
High-compression selection removes easy examples needed to calibrate broad class regions.
The scoring probe costs as much as the model whose training is supposedly saved.
A score aligned to one architecture or target fails for a different downstream model.
Repeated epochs over a small retained subset overfit and erase compute gains.
The fitted exponential region crosses back to a power law as the source pool grows.
reusable_insights: Always label the resource axis: retained examples, inspected examples, unique tokens, scoring compute, and training compute yield different scaling claims.
A fixed pruning fraction cannot change the asymptotic exponent in the paper's own model; adaptive fraction is the operative intervention.
Selection-score quality should be stress-tested by deliberately weakening the probe and locating the crossover.
Data pruning needs distribution, subgroup, OOD, and calibration audits, not only aggregate accuracy.
open_questions: Can an end-to-end compute-optimal law include source acquisition, scoring, storage, and repeated downstream reuse?
Which scores transfer across architectures, tasks, and modalities without target labels?
Can randomized or coverage-constrained selection avoid high-compression distribution shift while retaining an exponent gain?
How should a pruning frontier be estimated prospectively without choosing the best fraction on the test curve?
Do similar effects persist for next-token pretraining where examples are dependent and difficulty is context-specific?

competitive_landscape.title: Data pruning and neural scaling laws: fundamental limitations of score-based algorithms
competitive_landscape.difference: Ayed and Hayou prove no-free-lunch results and distribution-shift failures for score-based pruning at high compression, directly challenging the high-quality-score assumption needed for the reviewed exponential frontier.

competitive_landscape.title: Mind the Boundary: Coreset Selection via Reconstructing the Decision Boundary
competitive_landscape.difference: Yang et al. explicitly reconstruct the decision boundary and report 50% ImageNet pruning with less than one accuracy point loss, substantially beyond the reviewed prototype metric's headline 20%.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards Sustainable Learning: Coresets for Data-efficient Deep Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: CREST supplies nonconvex-training guarantees and an adaptive pipeline that excludes already learned examples; the reviewed work focuses on static ranking and retained-data scaling.

competitive_landscape.title: Lightweight Dataset Pruning without Full Training via Example Difficulty and Prediction Uncertainty
competitive_landscape.difference: Cho et al. target the omitted selection-cost axis and report ImageNet results at 90% pruning without full probe training; the reviewed method assumes a pretrained SWaV embedding or expensive supervised scores.

competitive_landscape.title: Coresets for Data-efficient Training of Machine Learning Models
competitive_landscape.difference: CRAIG selects subsets to approximate full gradient dynamics with theoretical convergence motivation; the reviewed paper instead selects individual difficulty scores to alter the data-scaling envelope.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Appropriate data pruning can replace slow power-law error scaling with exponential or faster retained-data scaling and motivate reusable foundation datasets.
novelty_assessment.evidence: A solvable perceptron yields the mechanism, vision sweeps reproduce qualitative Pareto behavior, and a prototype score saves 20% of ImageNet while maintaining accuracy.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The adaptive-retention Pareto perspective and probe-quality crossover are valuable. The strongest scaling language is conditional on an excellent selector and a retained-example accounting that omits the larger source pool; subsequent theory exposes high-compression limits, while later methods improve practical ImageNet pruning.

reviewer_notes: Read all 53 extracted pages, including theory derivations, scaling-fit appendix, resource tradeoffs, OOD and fairness audits, and numerical tables. Direct critiques and later coreset methods were checked at primary arXiv and PMLR records on 2026-08-23.
